The European anchovy Engraulis encrasicolus begins life as a transparent, yolk-sac larva emerging from a pelagic egg after a brief incubation period. At the moment of eclosion, the prolarva measures approximately 0.3 cm [Lb = approximately 0.3 cm] in standard length, a size that represents the mid-range of the smaller size class with gut content documented in field-collected specimens. This initial length corresponds to a remarkably low dry weight at birth, calculated from the allometric relationship established by Catalán and Folkvord using field data: the ln of dry weight in micrograms equals 0.867 plus half the standard length in millimeters, yielding a dry weight of approximately 0.00000053 grams  for a neonate of this length. The chorion rupture occurs roughly 6 days [ab = roughly 6 days] after fertilisation when the water temperature is maintained at 19 °C [T = 19 °C], a thermal condition typical of spring spawning grounds in the Mediterranean basin. During this endotrophic phase, the prolarva relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves, while its transparent body and undeveloped mouthparts preclude any exogenous feeding.

As the yolk-sac larva progresses through the lecithotrophic stage, rapid morphological changes prepare it for the transition to exogenous feeding. Under continued thermal conditions of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], the timing of metamorphosis is notably consistent: larvae undergo the larval-juvenile transition at approximately 60 days  after hatching, a developmental milestone marked by the onset of scale formation and fin ray ossification. At this metamorphic climax, individuals have attained a standard length of 3.75 cm , which corresponds to a dry weight of 0.0007 times the standard length raised to the power of 4.2395, yielding roughly 0.0018 grams  based on the Ifremer Juvesu 1999 survey of juveniles ranging from 3 to 4.4 cm standard length. This allometric shift reflects a fundamental reorganisation of body plan, enabling the post-larva to exploit planktonic prey resources more effectively. The completion of yolk-sac resorption and the onset of first exogenous feeding occur shortly before this transformation, marking a critical trophic switch in the life history.

Sexual maturation in the European anchovy follows a protracted developmental trajectory influenced by regional thermal regimes. Off the western Portuguese coast, where the average sea surface temperature is 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the age at first reproduction is approximately 292 days after hatching [tR = approximately 292 days after hatching], a value derived from field observations of gonadal recrudescence and the onset of spawning activity. At this stage, individuals have reached a standard length at puberty of 9 cm [Lp = 9 cm], a size at which the wet weight at puberty is estimated from PELGAS survey data as 0.0041 times the standard length raised to 3.2099, yielding roughly 4.7 grams [Wwp = roughly 4.7 grams]. This mass already incorporates the reproductive buffer typical of iteroparous spawning adults. The protracted nature of this maturation reflects the energetic demands of somatic growth prior to the initiation of vitellogenesis and spermiation, a pattern consistent with other small pelagic clupeiforms inhabiting temperate upwelling systems.

Adult European anchovies exhibit a relatively compressed lifespan compared to larger teleosts, with the maximum recorded longevity in the wild typically reaching 5 years [am = 5 years] at an ambient water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], though exceptionally old individuals have been documented at up to 13 years in some survey records. The ultimate total length attained by sexually mature Age 3 individuals during spring 2000 Ifremer PELGAS surveys is 18 cm [Li = 18 cm], a measurement taken as total length. This asymptotic size corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 0.0041 times the total length raised to 3.2099, yielding approximately 43.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 43.9 grams] based on the allometric relationship derived from those same surveys. The species is iteroparous, with spawning adults capable of producing multiple batches of eggs per season. At a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females produce approximately 20 batches of eggs per year [F_R_i = approximately 20 batches of eggs per year], each batch containing roughly 16,425 eggs [N_R_i = each batch containing roughly 16,425 eggs], a reproductive strategy that compensates for high larval mortality.

The ecological role of Engraulis encrasicolus as a planktivorous forage fish is tightly coupled to its life history parameters, which in turn shape its population dynamics and responses to environmental variability. The extremely low dry weight at birth of 0.00000053 grams  underscores the extreme vulnerability of early life stages to starvation and predation, a constraint that selects for the high fecundity observed in this species. At metamorphosis, the dry weight of roughly 0.0018 grams  represents a several-thousand-fold increase over the birth mass, reflecting the rapid growth rates possible under favourable planktonic conditions. The estimated maximum lifespan of 5 years [am = 5 years] in wild populations, combined with the relatively early attainment of a standard length of 9 cm [Lp = 9 cm] at puberty and a corresponding wet weight at puberty of 4.7 grams [Wwp = 4.7 grams], describes a life history strategy characterised by early maturation and high reproductive output at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This pattern is typical of small pelagic clupeiforms that experience high natural mortality rates and must compensate through rapid population turnover, a dynamic of considerable importance for the sustainable management of this commercially valuable species in the Mediterranean and adjacent Atlantic waters.
